procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 10, 1960 of the Madras High Court in C.C.C.A. No. 90 of 1957.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The City Civil Judge initially ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. The High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit, holding that it was not maintainable.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, disagreeing with the High Court's decision, appealed to the Supreme Court.

directions: In accordance with the opinion of the Majority the appeal is allowed.
There will be a decree in favour of the plaintiffs as prayed for with costs throughout.

issue.issue_text: Whether a civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging a tax assessment on the ground that the statutory provision under which the assessment was made is ultra vires the legislature.

law.law_text: A civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit questioning the order of a statutory tribunal if the tribunal acts in violation of the statute's provisions or acts ultra vires (beyond) its powers.
An ultra vires statutory provision is considered legally non-existent and not a part of the act at all.
Authorities created by a statute (like a taxing authority) cannot rule on the validity of the very statute that gives them their power and existence.

application.application_text: The Court reasoned that when a taxing authority makes an assessment based on a provision that is ultra vires the legislature, it is relying on a provision that is legally non-existent.
By doing so, the authority is not acting "under the Act" but is traveling beyond the valid provisions of the Act. This is considered an act in excess of its jurisdiction.

The Court also found that the internal appeal machinery provided by a tax act is not the proper forum for such a challenge. It would be inappropriate for authorities who are "creatures" of the act to decide whether the act itself is valid.
Because the assessment is not truly "under the Act" but is an action in excess of jurisdiction, any statutory clause that bars civil court lawsuits does not apply.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a civil court does have jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging a tax assessment on the grounds that the underlying statutory provision is ultra vires. The Court's reasoning was that an assessment based on an invalid, non-existent provision is an act in excess of the taxing authority's jurisdiction, and therefore the civil court's power to review such an action is not excluded by the statute.

issue.issue_text: Whether a taxing authority, constituted under a statute, can entertain a plea and decide on the constitutional validity or vires of the provisions of the very statute it is charged with administering.

facts: The case presented the question of whether a taxing authority, which is created by a specific statute, has the power to consider and rule on a challenge to the constitutional validity (vires) of the very statute it is supposed to enforce.
law: The fundamental principle applied by the court is that a statutory authority is a 'creature of the statute' under which it is established.
An authority or tribunal created by a statute cannot question the validity or vires of the provisions of that statute.
The function of such an authority is to administer the law as it is written, not to sit in judgment over its constitutionality.
application: The Court reasoned that since the taxing authority derives its existence and all its powers from the statute, it cannot entertain a plea that a part of that statute is invalid.
The authority must 'take the statute as he finds it' and presume its validity.
The Court stated that it is not the 'province of the department or even the statutory Tribunal' to entertain objections that a piece of legislation is ultra vires or unconstitutional.
If such a challenge is raised before the taxing authority, it must be ignored, as the authority cannot grant relief by declaring the law invalid.
The proper forum for challenging the constitutionality of a statute is a court of law (like a High Court or the Supreme Court), not the administrative body charged with implementing it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a taxing authority, being a creature of the statute it administers, cannot entertain a plea or decide on the constitutional validity of the provisions of that statute. Its role is to apply the law as it stands, not to question its legality.

issue.issue_text: Whether a statutory provision barring suits to set aside or modify any assessment made "under this Act" ousts the jurisdiction of the civil court when the assessment is based on a charging section that is ultra vires.

facts: A party challenged a tax assessment in a civil court, arguing that the charging section of the statute under which the assessment was made was 'ultra vires' (i.e., beyond the constitutional power of the legislature).

The government argued that the suit was barred by a statutory provision stating, "No suit or other proceeding shall, except as expressly provided in this Act, be instituted in any court to set aside or modify any assessment made under this Act."
law: An authority created by a statute cannot question the 'vires' (validity) of that statute or its provisions; it must act under the assumption that the Act is valid.
An 'ultra vires' provision of a statute is considered legally non-existent and not a part of the Act.
A civil court's jurisdiction can only be ousted by express provision or necessary implication. Statutes that limit a court's jurisdiction are construed narrowly.
A civil court will always have jurisdiction to question the order of a statutory tribunal if that tribunal acts outside the Act, abuses its power, or acts in excess of its jurisdiction.
application: The Court focused on the interpretation of the phrase "under this Act" in the barring provision.

It reasoned that if a charging section is 'ultra vires', it is legally a nullity and not part of the Act. Therefore, any assessment based on that provision cannot be considered an assessment made "under this Act."

The Court held that the assessing authority's jurisdiction is limited to acting according to the *valid* provisions of the Act. When the authority relies on an 'ultra vires' provision, it "travels beyond the valid provisions" and acts "in excess of its jurisdiction."
Because the assessment was based on an invalid provision, it was deemed to be an action 'outside the Act'.
Consequently, the statutory bar, which only applies to assessments made "under this Act," was found to be inapplicable to this situation, and the jurisdiction of the civil court was not ousted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the statutory bar ousted the civil court's jurisdiction. It held that an assessment based on an 'ultra vires' charging section is not an assessment made "under this Act." Such an assessment is made outside the Act and in excess of the authority's jurisdiction, and therefore, a civil suit to challenge its validity is maintainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging a tax assessment on the ground that the statutory provision under which the assessment was made is ultra vires the legislature.
appellant_arguments: A civil court has jurisdiction to hear a suit challenging a tax assessment when the basis of the challenge is that the underlying statutory provision is unconstitutional or ultra vires.
respondent_arguments: The civil court's jurisdiction is ousted because the tax statute itself provides a complete machinery for challenging the correctness of an assessment and explicitly bars such suits in civil courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a taxing authority, constituted under a statute, can entertain a plea and decide on the constitutional validity or vires of the provisions of the very statute it is charged with administering.
appellant_arguments: A taxing authority, being a creature of a statute, cannot entertain a plea or decide on the constitutional validity of the very provisions it is tasked with administering. Such a question is beyond its jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The machinery provided under the statute is comprehensive, and therefore, all challenges, including the question of a provision's validity, should be raised before the statutory authorities.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a statutory provision barring suits to set aside or modify any assessment made "under this Act" ousts the jurisdiction of the civil court when the assessment is based on a charging section that is ultra vires.
appellant_arguments: The bar on suits does not apply because an assessment based on an ultra vires provision is a nullity and is not considered an assessment made "under this Act" in the eyes of the law.
respondent_arguments: The statutory bar on suits is absolute and prevents civil courts from hearing any challenge to an assessment, which must instead be pursued through the remedies provided within the Act itself.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An authority or tribunal which is a creature of a statute cannot decide upon the constitutional validity of that statute or its provisions.
obiter: The Privy Council took the view that the constitutional validity of a taxing provision can be challenged by adopting the procedure prescribed by the statute itself.
In a previous case, the Federal Court was bound by the decision of the Privy Council.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A civil court's jurisdiction is not ousted by a statutory provision that bars suits to set aside assessments made 'under the Act' when the challenge is to the constitutional validity of the charging provision itself. An assessment made under an ultra vires provision is a nullity and is not considered an assessment 'under the Act'. Consequently, since a statutory tribunal, being a creature of the statute, cannot entertain a plea questioning the vires of the very act it administers, the civil court remains the proper forum for such a challenge.
legal_tests_applied: The court applies a jurisdictional test based on the distinction between an erroneous assessment made within the authority of a valid statute and an assessment that is a nullity because it is based on a statutory provision that is ultra vires the legislature. An action taken under an ultra vires provision is considered to be outside the Act, and any statutory bar on civil suits for actions taken 'under this Act' does not apply.
policy_considerations: The court implicitly relies on the policy that a subject must have a legal forum to challenge the constitutionality of a law imposing a tax. If the specialized tribunals created by the statute are barred from hearing such a fundamental challenge, the jurisdiction of the ordinary civil courts to do so must be preserved to prevent a failure of justice.
